title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident illustrates AI-enabled impersonation used as an instrument of financial fraud. Scammers produced a fabricated news article containing an invented interview with two real public figures, a finance presenter and a central bank governor, to lend false credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure mode is straightforward: generative AI tools lowered the cost and skill required to produce convincing fake text, images, and video, making it practical to construct layered deceptions involving fake websites, fake articles, and fake advertisements together rather than a single forged image.

The deployment context is outside any single platform's control. The content was not generated within a regulated service and then misused; it was created by external actors and distributed through ordinary web infrastructure. Catching it would have required either proactive detection by the platforms hosting the content, the kind of regulatory takedown effort that ASIC describes, or authentication systems that could confirm whether a named journalist or official actually participated in a given interview. None of those mechanisms stopped the content from circulating.

What is not established is that any specific AI company or product was responsible for producing the fake material, and the reporting does not identify who created or operated the Boulder Sparhaven platform.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring an invented interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock highlights a growing scam trend. The fabricated piece described Bullock becoming angry during discussion of Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians are becoming more common and sophisticated due to artificial intelligence technology.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Alan Kohler, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and wealthy individuals like Gina Rinehart appear frequently in these impersonations. Rather than using single fake images, scammers now create complex webs of deception involving fake websites, news articles, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that online searches alone cannot confirm legitimacy.
